support.reconciliation:
The tradition has two main branches, and they reconcile the hard texts differently, chiefly by which texts they accept.

1. Texts every branch accepts (the Gathas and the Yasna Haptanghaiti, Tier 1). The Gathas repeatedly condemn fury (aēšma) and cruelty as the choice of the false gods (Yasna 29.1, 30.6, 49.4; 48.7 with verse number unverified), but no verse found says that no one may be killed. The same Gathas commend harming the follower of the Lie by word, thought or hand (Yasna 33.2 in Mills), call for resisting him with the weapon (31.18), and pray that death come through good rulers on raiders and persecutors (53.8 to 9). Reformists (the modern Gathas-only movement) reconcile this by reading the follower of the Lie as a moral type that anyone can choose or leave, and by rendering the hard verses as opposing wrongdoing: the Zarathushtrian Assembly's translation (A. A. Jafarey; stated to follow Humbach with emendations) has 'foils the wrongful' at 33.2, and WZSE 255 on avesta.org reads 31.18 as resistance with spiritual weapons. These are modern translators and an organisation, not an authorised interpreting body, and they do not agree among themselves: D. J. Irani keeps 'force' at 31.18, and F. Azargoshasb keeps fighting the wicked with arms at 33.2. No reformist statement on killing as such was found.

2. Traditionalists (orthodox Parsi priesthood and Iranian traditionalists) accept the whole Avesta, including the Vendidad (Tier 1, contested), and read it through the Pahlavi books, which they hold as the authoritative interpretation of scripture though not as revelation (Tier 2, not counted under METHOD.md section 9, decision 4). The Vendidad punishes a blow that kills any person (Fargard 4), a law that teaches K1 for this branch, though with a light penalty (graded protection, rule 2). The Pahlavi books state the line the tradition itself draws: killing driven by passion is unlawful and demonic, and lawful killing is only of those sentenced by the religion and the king (Denkard 3, chapter 388 or 387); death and mutilation may not be inflicted until the ruler decrees, and whoever punishes on his own authority is like a highway robber (Denkard 5); killing men without justice is a sin needing atonement (Denkard 5); slaying a righteous man is the third most heinous of thirty sins (Menog-i Khrad 36). On this classical reading, any capital rulings in the Vendidad are judicial (context, rule 5), and private killing is forbidden. Two limits remain in the same Tier 2 texts: protection is framed for the righteous (Menog-i Khrad 36; the unverified 'virtuous men' chapter), and turning away from God is treated as a capital matter for religious and royal courts (Denkard 3). Both limit equal protection; neither permits private killing.

Standing of the authorities: Gathas, counted for all branches; Younger Avesta and Vendidad, counted for traditionalists only; Denkard and Menog-i Khrad, classical Tier 2 authority for traditionalists, which may narrow a reading (rule 6) but cannot decide a label alone (rule 1); modern translators, reformist voices without official standing. No statement by a present-day authoritative body (Parsi high priests, an Iranian council of mobeds, or FEZANA) on killing was searched.

K1.label: Unclear (rule 6), provisional
K1.reason: In the texts every branch accepts (the Gathas), K1 is not taught: the condemnations of fury and violence (Yasna 29.1, 30.6, 49.4, 32.11) are Implied, and 48.7 is unverified. Yasna 33.2 (Mills) commends private persons harming the follower of the Lie 'with both hands'; it bears directly on K1's protection of 'the wicked', but it does not name killing and translators divide on whether its object is people, so its reach is unresolved (rule 6, as in the households annex for L1). Yasna 31.18 and 53.8 to 9 are defence or rulers' force (exception or context, rule 5). For traditionalists, Vendidad 4 teaches K1 at Clear teaching, and the Pahlavi books (Tier 2, not counted) explicitly confine lawful killing to sentence by religion and king and liken private punishment to highway robbery. Under the branch rule this cannot make K1 taught for the whole tradition, so even if 33.2 were resolved the reformist way, the best result would be 'taught in one branch (traditionalists)'. Provisional because I did not check the Vendidad passages that may approve killing certain classes of people (see gaps): if one lets private persons kill, the traditionalist result would be 'contradicted in one branch', or Unclear if its judicial character is disputed or Denkard 5's rule is taken to narrow it (rules 3, 5 and 6).

K0.label: Taught in one branch only (traditionalists); not taught for the whole tradition (Implied in the Gathas)
K0.reason: Traditionalists: Vendidad 4 (Tier 1, contested) punishes killing a person by a blow whatever the motive, which teaches K0 as a wider rule (Clear teaching), and Denkard 3 (Tier 2, not counted) states explicitly that killing driven by passion is unlawful and demonic. Gathas (all branches): fury against human life is the false gods' choice (30.6) and fury is to be put down (48.7, verse unverified). That is at best borderline Clear teaching for the anger clause only, so at most taught in part; nothing in the Gathas addresses killing for gain, hatred or revenge above the Implied level (32.11). Yasna 33.2 names no motive of gain, anger, hatred or revenge, so it does not bear directly on K0. Under the branch rule, a result for traditionalists alone does not make K0 taught for the tradition.

K3.label: Silent (in the counted texts searched)
K3.reason: No counted text found says to spare non-combatants, children, the old or those who surrender. The Gathic texts on force (31.18; 53.8 to 9) concern resisting raiders and persecutors through rulers or the community, with no word on non-combatants. The Yashts' prayers for victory over enemies (for example Yasht 5, 10 and 19) were not checked in this run, and no Pahlavi text on the conduct of war was searched, so silence rests on a thin search.

counter.reconciliation: Zoroastrianism has no single authorised interpreting body, so its reconciliations come from its branches. (1) The Gathas, Tier 1 for every branch. Yasna 31.18 sets its call to resist 'with the weapon' against a follower of the Lie who brings house, village and land to ruin and death. Yasna 53.8 gives death and bloodshed to evil-doers 'through good rulers' for the peace of the villages. On their own terms, then, the Gathas tie force to defence and to rule. Yasna 33.2 (harming the follower of the Lie by word, thought or hand) and 47.4 (hostility to him) name no killing. (2) Reformists (the 'Gathas-only' movement; modern teachers and translators such as the Zarathushtrian Assembly and A. A. Jafarey's translation, D. J. Irani, Dina McIntyre, and the Weekly Zoroastrian Scripture Extracts on avesta.org; none of them an authorised body) hold that the Vendidad is a later priestly text with no binding force. So its death sentences do not bind them. They read the follower of the Lie as a moral choice anyone may make or leave (resting on Yasna 30.2 to 3; not verified). They read the weapon of 31.18 as spiritual (WZSE 255), 33.1 to 2 as equal treatment with a duty to guide the corrupt (WZSE 219), and 53.8 as good rule that prevents war (Zarathushtrian Assembly). They are not uniform: Irani renders 31.18 'grip your sword and cut them down' and keeps rejection at 47.4, and F. Azargoshasb keeps 'fighting the wicked' at 33.2. (3) Traditionalists (the Parsi priesthood and Iranian mobeds) accept the Vendidad as scripture and read it through the Pahlavi books, which they hold as the authoritative interpretation but not as revelation. On that reading, the Vendidad's only express death sentences, for the false cleanser (9.47 to 57) and for the man who carries a corpse alone (3.14 to 21), are religious-law punishments ordered by 'the worshippers of Mazda' as a body (Darmesteter, Introduction to SBE 4: outside the corpus, 19th-century scholarship). The wider category of sins 'worthy of death' (margarzān, also used of the peshotanu) was read down to two hundred strokes (Darmesteter, reporting the tradition). A Denkard passage reported in a secondary source, unverified, has the mortal sinner confess to the high priests and hand over his body and wealth to them, which would place capital sins under priestly-judicial authority. Repentance (patet) was held to save the sinner before God but not to remove the earthly penalty (Darmesteter). Against this, Darmesteter's French note on Fargard 1 reports a tradition that for a capital crime 'the first comer' may kill the offender, and Wikipedia reports commentary allowing those who commit sodomy (Vendidad 8.32) to be killed without the Dastur's permission. The source of that tradition (Pahlavi Zand, Sad Dar or Persian Rivayats) was not identified, and none of these is counted. M. N. Dhalla (Parsi high priest and scholar, 1938; outside the corpus) says the ancient texts made heresy a crime punishable by law, with the severity much reduced in the Sasanian period. Standing summary: Gathas, counted for all; Vendidad and Younger Avesta, counted for traditionalists only; Pahlavi books, Tier 2 and not counted (decision 4); Persian Rivayats, Sad Dar, Darmesteter, Dhalla and the WZSE series, outside the corpus. No present-day statement by a Parsi or Iranian priestly council on the Vendidad's death penalties or on Yasna 33.2 was searched for.

K1.label: Unclear (rules 5 and 6); not contradicted by any verified counted text
K1.reason: No verified counted text was found that lets a private person kill someone who is not attacking. In the Gathas (all branches), Yasna 33.2 commends harming the follower of the Lie 'with both hands' and Yasna 31.18 calls for resistance 'with the weapon'. Whether these reach killing a non-attacker turns on disputed words (drəgvant; the weapon) and on readings that the tradition's own interpreters narrow in opposite directions (rule 6). 31.18's most natural reading is defence, inside K1's exception, and 33.2 names no killing. If the project judges both that way, the Gathic counter side is clear, and the label falls to whatever the support evidence shows; Article I row 3f found only Implied Gathic teaching. In the Vendidad (traditionalists only), the death sentences for the false cleanser (9.47 to 57) and the lone corpse-carrier (3.14 to 21) are best read as communal punishment under religious law, context (a). But the text names no court, and a later tradition (not counted) let 'the first comer' kill some 'worthy of death' offenders. Vendidad 18.61 to 65 may call for killing the Jahi, with no actor named, but the kill clause is unverified and her human or demonic status is disputed. If the Pahlavi source of the private-killing tradition were identified and counted, K1 would become 'contradicted in one branch (traditionalist)'.

K0.label: Not contradicted; taught in one branch (traditionalist, Vendidad 4 as a wider rule); Gathas only Implied (silent at the counted level for reformists)
K0.reason: No counted text was found permitting killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge. Vendidad Fargard 4 makes striking any person with evil intent a graded offence, a wider duty not to harm anyone that reaches killing out of anger or hatred (rule 7): Clear teaching for traditionalists only. The Gathas condemn fury and cruelty (Yasna 29.1, 30.6, 49.4) only at the Implied level. Yasna 33.2 and 47.4 commend harm and hostility towards the follower of the Lie, framed as service to God, not as anger or revenge, and name no killing: Implied, not contradiction.

K3.label: Silent (no verified counted text either way; Yashts not checked)
K3.reason: Yasna 31.18 (armed resistance) and 53.8 (death to evil-doers through good rulers) concern defence and rule and say nothing about non-combatants. The Younger Avesta Yashts (5, 10, 19), which pray for victory and describe smiting enemies, could not be searched once the shared search budget ran out. No counted text was found either protecting or targeting people who are not fighting.

verified.reconciliation:
Zoroastrianism has no authorised interpreting body. Its two main branches reconcile the hard texts mainly by which texts they accept.

(1) Gathas (counted for every branch). The Gathas condemn fury and cruelty as the false gods' choice (Yasna 30.6, 29.1, 49.4; 48.7 unverified), but no verse found says that no one may be killed. The same Gathas commend harming the follower of the Lie by word, thought or hand (33.2, in Mills), call on all hearers to resist him with the weapon (31.18), set hostility to him as a norm (47.4, unverified; 43.8; 46.6), and pray for death on raiders and persecutors through good rulers (53.8 to 9, context). On their own terms they tie armed force to those who bring ruin and death to house and village (31.18) and to rule (53.8).

Reformists (the Gathas-only movement) read the follower of the Lie as a moral choice anyone may make or leave (resting on Yasna 30.2 to 3, unverified). They read the weapon of 31.18 as spiritual (WZSE 255) and 33.1 to 2 as equal treatment with a duty to guide the corrupt (WZSE 219). These are modern teachers and translators, not an authorised body, and they do not agree among themselves: Irani keeps the sword at 31.18 and Azargoshasb keeps fighting the wicked at 33.2. Their readings therefore show that the words are disputed (rule 6). They do not settle the dispute.

(2) Traditionalists (orthodox Parsi priesthood and Iranian traditionalists) also count the Younger Avesta and the Vendidad. They read these through the Pahlavi books, which they hold as authoritative interpretation but not revelation (Tier 2, uncounted under decision 4). The Vendidad makes malicious assault on any person a graded offence (Fargard 4). Its few express death sentences (the lone corpse-carrier, 3.14 to 21; the false cleanser, 9.47 to 57; both unverified by this verifier) are ordered by 'the worshippers of Mazda' as religious-law penalties. The Pahlavi books draw the line rule 5 draws: killing from passion is unlawful and demonic, and lawful killing comes only by sentence of religion and king (Denkard 3). No one may inflict death or mutilation until the ruler decrees, and whoever punishes on his own authority is like a highway robber (Denkard 5). Killing men without justice is a sin needing atonement (Denkard 5), and slaying a righteous man is the third most heinous of thirty sins (Menog-i Khrad 36). All of these are unverified here and uncounted.

Against this stands a later tradition, reported by Darmesteter and Wikipedia but with its source unidentified, that 'the first comer' may kill a margarzān offender, and that those who commit sodomy may be killed without the high priest's leave. Vendidad 18.65 may say the Jahi should be killed more than snakes and wolves (kill clause unverified; whether she is human or demonic is disputed).

Standing: Gathas, counted for all; Younger Avesta and Vendidad, counted for traditionalists only; Pahlavi books, classical authority for traditionalists but uncounted (they can narrow under rule 6, never decide); Darmesteter, Dhalla, the WZSE series and the reformist translators are outside the corpus. No present-day statement by Parsi high priests, an Iranian council of mobeds or FEZANA on killing was searched for.

K1.label: Unclear (rule 6)
K1.reason: Counted texts accepted by every branch bear directly on K1, but their reach is unresolved. Yasna 31.18 calls on all hearers, not rulers, to resist the follower of the Lie 'with the weapon'. Its target (attackers who bring ruin and death, or anyone who teaches the Lie) and its weapon (literal or spiritual) are disputed words, and its most natural literal reading falls within K1's exception or is communal war. Yasna 33.2 commends harming the follower of the Lie 'with both hands'. It names no killing, and translators divide on whether its object is people or evil. Both texts concern private persons, so rule 5 does not exclude them. Neither verified text approves killing a non-attacker, so K1 is not contradicted. Support in the Gathas is only Implied (30.6, 29.1, 49.4; 48.7 unverified), so K1 is not taught for the whole tradition. For traditionalists only, the Vendidad's assault law (Fargard 4, annex ZO-3) teaches K1 as a wider rule at Clear teaching, provisionally. Its reach to non-Mazdeans is not stated (the Vendidad 7 lead suggests graded protection by faith). The Vendidad's death sentences (3.14 to 21; 9.47 to 57) are context (a) on the judicial reading, which the traditionalists' own Denkard 5 supports. Two things could make the traditionalist result Unclear or 'contradicted in one branch' (rules 3 and 5): Vendidad 18.65's kill clause, if verified and read as a human woman, and the uncounted 'first comer' tradition, if shown to govern counted offences. Dependency: if the project rules that neither 31.18 nor 33.2 reaches killing a non-attacker, the label becomes 'not contradicted; taught in one branch only (traditionalists, provisionally); Implied only in the Gathas'. The label rests only on rows verified in committed project records (33.2: annex ZO-14; 31.18: ZA-10 and Article I section G), not on any row this verifier downgraded.

K0.label: Taught in one branch only (traditionalists); not taught in texts every branch accepts (Gathas: Implied only); not contradicted
K0.reason: Traditionalists: Vendidad Fargard 4 (Tier 1 for that branch; annex ZO-3, verified in a committed record) makes striking any person with evil intent a graded offence. That is a wider duty not to assault anyone, which reaches killing for gain or out of anger, hatred or revenge (rule 7, Clear teaching). The 'gives up the ghost' grade would add to this if confirmed, but it is unverified and its meaning is in doubt. Denkard 3 states explicitly that killing from passion is unlawful, but it is Tier 2 and uncounted (rule 1). Gathas (all branches): fury against human life is the false gods' choice (30.6), and 48.7's call to put fury down is unverified. That is at best borderline Clear teaching for the anger clause only, so taught in part at most, and nothing addresses gain, hatred or revenge above the Implied level (32.11, unverified). No counted text permits killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge. Yasna 33.2 and 47.4 frame hostility to the follower of the Lie as service to God, not as anger or revenge. Whether religious enmity counts as 'hatred' under K0 should be decided once for all traditions; if it does, 33.2 would make K0 Unclear as it does K1. Yasht 9.18's royal revenge killing (unverified) is war or ruler context and does not decide. Under the branch rule, a result for traditionalists alone does not make K0 taught for the whole tradition.

K3.label: Silent
K3.reason: No counted text, verified or unverified, was found that protects or targets non-combatants, children, the old or those who surrender in war. The Gathic texts on force (31.18; 53.8 to 9) concern resisting raiders and persecutors and say nothing on non-combatants. The Younger Avesta Yashts that pray for victory (5, 10, 19) and Yasht 9.18 (a royal revenge killing in the Iran and Turan war) are unverified leads and are context (b) only. No Pahlavi text on the conduct of war was searched. So the silence rests on a thin search.

verified.fairness_notes:
1. The dog comparison. Saying the Vendidad punishes killing a person far less than killing a dog rests on Darmesteter's 'gives up the ghost'. That rendering may mean loss of consciousness, and Darmesteter himself thought the dog penalties were never applied. Stated baldly, it would read to an adherent as ridicule, so it should appear only with these caveats.

2. Old base translations. The hardest Gathic verses (33.2, 31.18) are judged on Mills (1887) and on Bartholomae through a 1951 English, while Insler (1975) and Humbach (1991) have not been read. If other traditions' hard verses are judged on modern critical translations, Zoroastrianism is held to an older and harsher text. The Unclear label rests on the words being disputed, which is fair either way, but this gap should be closed.

3. No classical commentators for reformists. Rule 6 lets classical commentators narrow a reading, and the reformist branch, being modern, has none, so its readings can enter only as evidence that a word is disputed. That is not unfair if the same is done for modern readings in other traditions, but it should be stated.

4. Communal executions. The Vendidad's executions ordered by 'the worshippers of Mazda' are treated as court context. Other traditions' communal or congregational executions (for example, a whole congregation carrying out a legal death sentence) must be classified the same way, whichever way is chosen.

5. The Jahi passage. It should not be summarised as 'the Vendidad orders women killed' unless the kill clause is verified, and even then only with the dispute over whether the Jahi is a demoness or a human woman.

6. Uncounted texts on both sides. The Pahlavi books' explicit condemnations of unlawful and private killing (Denkard 3 and 5; Menog-i Khrad 36) are uncounted, and so is the reported 'first comer' tradition. Neither should colour the label more than the other. Decision 4 leaves Zoroastrianism's main ethical literature uncounted, as it does the Mahabharata and the Five Classics. An adherent may feel this understates the tradition, but the rule is applied the same way to all.

7. Zeal and hatred. Yasna 33.2 and 47.4 are read as not bearing on K0 because they frame hostility as service to God, not as hatred. Zealot texts in other traditions should be read the same way.

8. Procedural downgrades. This verifier could not search. Rows marked UNVERIFIED for that reason only (for example Vendidad 3, 9 and 15, Denkard 3 and 5, and Menog-i Khrad 36) should not be read as findings against the texts or the researchers, and other traditions' rows were verified with search budgets that this tradition's verifier did not get.
